episode_title: He Exiled His Own Father at 19 — and the Old Man Outlived Him: Takeda Shingen's Coldest Choice

youtube_description:
In the summer of 1541, a nineteen-year-old closed the road home to his own father, and the old man lived to outlast him. The chronicles name the son, but the valley behind him was struggling through hungry years. Would you have shut that road, or held it open?

📰 Your reporter: Tokio Kamiya, a former Tokyo foreign correspondent. His grandfather's brass pocket watch carries him to one day of Japan's past at a time. He can watch and he can speak, but he can never change what happens. Every episode is his dispatch from the scene.

🎌 Subscribe for new episodes 3 times a week:
https://www.youtube.com/@Samurai-Chronicles-JP

🌐 Official site: https://samurai-chronicles.com

🇯🇵 A Japanese perspective on Japanese history — created by a Japanese history enthusiast.

📚 References:
1. Sansom, George — "A History of Japan, 1334–1615" (Stanford University Press, 1961)
2. Yamamura, Kozo (ed.) — "The Cambridge History of Japan, Vol. 3: Medieval Japan" (Cambridge University Press, 1990)
3. Turnbull, Stephen — "Samurai Commanders (1): 940–1576" (Osprey Publishing, 2005)
4. Myōhōji-ki (Katsuyama-ki) and Enzan Kōgakuan shōnendaiki — Kai provincial chronicles (primary sources, consulted in modern editions)

teaser_narration: The Kai-Suruga border, summer 1541. I watch soldiers drag a barrier across the road, shutting a lord out of his own country. The records say the order came from his nineteen-year-old son. But a whole valley stood behind that gate. Whose decision was it?
shorts_narration: 19 years old. One road closed. His own father, locked out of Kai for good. The chronicles name the son, but who really shut the gate? And the old man outlived him anyway. This is Takeda Shingen.

scenes.narration: I should explain. I am a correspondent, or I was, until my grandfather's brass watch passed to me. It carries me to any moment in Japan's past, for one day at a time. I may watch. I may speak. I may not change a thing. Today it sets me down on a dirt road in the mountains of Kai, in the summer of 1541. A timber gate stands across it. By the end of this day, a father will lose a country. I have one day to learn who took it.

scenes.narration: Let me start with the father, because the story usually skips him. Takeda Nobutora is forty-seven. Kai has been torn by rival families for generations, and I read that around 1519 he is the man who finally ends it. He builds a new headquarters in the valley, the Tsutsujigasaki mansion, and a town grows around it, the one we now call Kofu. In 1537 he marries his daughter to Imagawa Yoshimoto, the young lord of Suruga. I think this is no weak man. He built what his son is about to take.

scenes.narration: Now the year. The records of a Kai temple tell me the harvests are bad in these seasons, and the valley is struggling. All the while Nobutora keeps marching his men north into Shinano. I read that in May of 1541 he fights at Unno-daira, only weeks before this day. The rice is thin, and the young men are away. I cannot give you a number for the hunger, and I will not invent one. I only note that a lord at war in a hungry valley is a lord people begin to count.

scenes.narration: And the son. Takeda Harunobu, who will one day take the name Shingen, is nineteen by the count a modern reader would use. By the count of his own day, which gives a baby a year at birth and another every New Year, he is twenty-one. I read that he was born in the last weeks of 1521. I have no portrait of him at this age, so I build him from the records: the heir of the house, trusted by senior men, and watchful. I look for him on this road, and I do not find him. I write that down.

scenes.narration: I walk back to Kofu, to the Tsutsujigasaki mansion, on the morning the old lord leaves. Nobutora rides out with a modest escort, bound south for Suruga, to visit his daughter and her husband Yoshimoto. I stand at the roadside among the merchants. The household bows. He looks at no one. If anyone in that courtyard knows what the road ahead holds, no one says so. I think it looks like a plain family visit, and that is exactly what troubles me. I watch him go.

scenes.narration: Behind him, the mansion changes hands without a word. The records name the senior retainers who side with the heir: Itagaki Nobukata and Amari Torayasu, two of the most senior men of the house. Here I must be careful. I can give you the names. I cannot give you the conversation. No one wrote down who said it first, who said it again, or who simply nodded. I stand in the corridors and hear only footsteps and the creak of old floors. I think they sound like men who have already decided.

scenes.narration: So who is behind this? I weigh three readings. One: the heir plots alone, an ambitious young man. That is how a later military book, the Koyo Gunkan, likes to tell it. Two: the senior retainers, worn down by war and hunger, choose a new lord, and the heir is their banner. Some modern historians lean this way. Three: Imagawa Yoshimoto agrees to take the old man in, perhaps even beforehand. He may have. No letter I can find says so. I cannot make these three fight to a single winner. They may all be partly true.

scenes.narration: Later the same day, an old rice porter at the edge of town told me, once I said I was a travelling merchant, that the old lord took the village's young men to Shinano twice, and the rice has been thin. He sets down his sack and rubs his shoulder. I ask who is lord now. He thinks for a long time, then shrugs. Whoever fills the granary, he says. He says nothing of hatred, and nothing of joy. I did not expect the quiet. I write it down.

scenes.narration: Far down that road, the old lord crosses into Suruga with his escort. The records say he is going to see his son-in-law, and his daughter, Lady Jokein. Then I read that the border is sealed behind him. A barrier goes up, and the way home is shut. Not by an enemy army, but by men of his own house, acting in his son's name. A father rides away calm. Behind him, a road becomes a wall. I have pictured this scene a hundred times, and it is never as quiet as this.

scenes.narration: I am back at the barrier now. Timber stakes, a rope, and a few armed men who will not meet my eyes. The old lord is already beyond them in Suruga, and these men have orders. The date the sources give is the fourteenth day of the sixth month, in the tenth year of Tenbun. Whose name is on the orders? The chronicles put the young heir's name on them. I wait for the gate to open. I wait a long time. It does not open. A father is a stranger in his own country. I check my watch. It does not move.

scenes.narration: Now I read what the nearest writers say. A temple chronicle in Kai records the change of lord and says, in words to that effect, that the whole province rejoiced. It was written inside Kai, after the change, and a new lord is always glad of a record that says his people were glad. The Koyo Gunkan, a military book from the next century, paints the old man as a monster, and I set it aside. The records speak in the son's name. Behind him stand tired retainers and a neighbour who may have agreed. I will not pick one.

scenes.narration: I leaf ahead in my notebook, because I know what comes next. Nobutora does not go back to Kai. Imagawa Yoshimoto takes his father-in-law in, and some records say Kai sends money for his keep. No one kills him. In the chronicles, the old man simply stops being a lord and becomes a guest. The next year, Harunobu is marching north into Shinano, and in time his name will frighten his neighbours. A son shuts one door, and a great many open.

scenes.narration: Then the trail thins. I read that the old lord leaves Suruga and goes to Kyoto, where he is said to move near the shogun's circle. More than that, I do not have. No diary of his survives that I can find. I will not fill the years with feelings for him. I only note the shape. A man who made a province lives out his days in other men's houses, and for more than thirty years I cannot quote a single line he wrote.

scenes.narration: Dusk at the barrier. The men have gone, and the stakes still stand. In the notebook I turn to the spring of 1573. Shingen, the son's name now, is fifty-one by the modern count, and on the road home from a long campaign, he dies. The army turns for home. I look at the empty road south and think of an old man hearing that news. How does a father learn that his exiled son is dead? I find no record of the words.

scenes.narration: The watch grows warm against my chest. I read the last entry. In 1573, with his son dead, an old man of about eighty is said to reach Takato, a mountain stronghold in Shinano tied to his grandson Katsuyori. By the spring of 1574 he is dead. The accounts of his journey differ, and I do not know which to trust. But the arithmetic is plain. The man shut out of Kai at forty-seven outlived the son who shut him out. I close the notebook gently.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. Back in my own century, I walk through Kofu, a city of nearly two hundred thousand people. It stands where the father put it. In its heart, the Takeda shrine occupies the ground of the old mansion, and it honours the son, not the father. A statue of Shingen greets travellers at the railway station. I stand in the grounds and think how few visitors know the founder's name. I think it is the quietest way to be exiled: a city that exists because of you, with someone else's statue at its door.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. Japan has an old, odd word for what may have happened here: oshikome. In later centuries, when a lord ruined his domain, his own retainers could quietly confine him and install his heir. It was not written in law, but it was often tolerated, because it kept the house alive. I think that is worth sitting with. The nineteen-year-old and the old men around him may have thought they were saving a house. Or they may not. And Shingen's own eldest son, Yoshinobu, was confined in 1567 and died that year. The causes are still argued.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. Here is my opinion, for what it is worth. I came to find the villain of a family drama, and I found three overlapping stories and one empty road. I do not think anyone can honestly say whether Shingen was the author or the instrument. Both may be true. A nineteen-year-old can carry out a decision that a valley has already made, and still be the one whose name goes on it. Japan remembers a tiger. I remember a young man at a rope, and an old man who lived to outlast him.

scenes.narration: That is all I can carry from the records: a gate, a name, and an old man's long wait. The rest is the question a nineteen-year-old left behind, and I will not answer it for him. In my grandfather's notebook, the page in my own handwriting still reads only 1868. Subscribe, and the next dispatch will find you. The watch is ticking. Until the next report. Tokio Kamiya, reporting.
